alternative: Compute the payload before delegation and pass it through a delegating constructor or a static factory: this(compute(args)) or super(compute(args)), then store the same value in a final field - or replace inheritance with composition. Java prohibits instance state in an explicit constructor invocation and offers no second class base to carry the based-member.
idiom_name: none - super(...) runs before field initializers and may not read instance state
implementation_notes: The Java Language Specification states the trap exactly: an explicit constructor invocation statement introduces a static context, so this and super are prohibited there along with unqualified references to instance variables and instance methods, and the instance variable initializers of the class run only after the superclass constructor completes. A base therefore cannot be initialised from the derived object's own data, and because a Java class has exactly one direct superclass (interfaces declare no instance state), there is no second base to move the member into - the structural hole the C++ idiom fills does not exist in Java at all. What replaces it is a value produced before delegation: a static helper or factory whose result is passed to super(...), a private delegating constructor that takes the payload as a parameter and exposes it as a final field, or composition when the inheritance is incidental.
pitfalls: super(...) or this(...) must be the constructor's first statement, so the payload has to be computable there - a static call or a constructor parameter; a value that needs the object's own state cannot be produced before delegation at all.

An overridden method called from the superclass constructor runs before the derived field initializers, so it observes null or 0; the compiler accepts this and reports nothing, which is exactly the silent failure the C++ idiom prevents by construction.

Records and final fields make the workaround worse: the payload must be assigned exactly once, so the delegating-constructor pattern is the only place it can be stored, and a second computation of the same value drifts unless it is factored out.
